name: Prohormones (1-Andro, 4-AD)

card.summary: Steroid precursors once sold as supplements; androstenedione was banned in the US in 2004 and studies found little muscle benefit.
card.note: Androstenedione is a controlled substance in the US since 2005 and banned by sports bodies.

quick.overview:
Prohormones are compounds that the body can convert into active hormones. In the 1990s, androstenedione (4-AD, called andro) was sold over the counter as a supplement for raising testosterone and building muscle, and gained fame through baseball players.

Studies found that a single large dose raised testosterone variably and that daily lower doses had no effect on strength, muscle size or body fat. The US classed it as an anabolic steroid in 2004.
quick.mechanism: Androstenedione is a precursor in the pathway to testosterone and estrogens. Oral doses may be converted to testosterone in some people, and estradiol also rose in studies.
quick.risks: The FDA banned its sale in 2004, and a 2004 US law added it to controlled-substance schedules, effective 2005. It is banned by the WADA, the Olympics and major sports leagues. Reported effects in women included masculinization and menstrual disturbance.

lead: Prohormones are precursor compounds that the body can convert into active hormones. In bodybuilding and physique-building culture the word usually means androstenedione (4-AD, or "andro") and relatives such as 1-androstenedione, sold over the counter in the 1990s and 2000s as testosterone boosters for people who wanted more muscle, a leaner build and a more muscular look.[1]

The appeal was a chain: if a supplement raised testosterone, users expected harder training, more lean mass and a more muscular physique. Androstenedione is an intermediate in the body's own pathway to testosterone and estrogens, and it was marketed on that basis. It was introduced to the North American market with credit given to Patrick Arnold, and gained fame through use by Major League Baseball players in the 1990s, including Mark McGwire.[1]

Published human studies examined whether the chain held. A 2000 JAMA study found that a single 300 mg oral dose raised serum testosterone in young men, with large individual differences and a rise in estradiol, while a 2006 review found that daily doses of 50 to 100 mg did not change strength, muscle size or body fat.[1] Regulators acted anyway: the IOC banned it in 1997, the FDA banned its sale in April 2004, and it became a US controlled substance in 2005.[1] Later designer prohormones remain discussed on T Nation, usually as a historical chapter of supplement culture.[2][3]

chain: Converted in part to testosterone or estrogens
More training capacity and lean mass, in users' expectation
angle.text: Users took prohormones hoping the conversion to testosterone would help them add muscle and lose fat for a bigger, leaner look. Studies of androstenedione measured testosterone and estradiol changes and tested strength and body-composition outcomes directly, and daily doses of 50 to 100 mg produced no change in those outcomes.[1]

infobox: Prohibited by WADA, IOC, MLB, NFL, NBA, NCAA

paras: In the supplement era, androstenedione was bought for muscle gain, strength and a leaner physique. Forum posters on T Nation describe classmates and gym acquaintances using prohormones as teenagers, and remember the 1990s baseball home-run era as the moment the products entered popular awareness.[2][4][5] Their reminiscences also mention later designer prohormones derived from other steroids, sold in the 2000s and since restricted.

Through the 1990s androstenedione was legal and sold as a dietary supplement. From 1996 to 2001, Barry McCaffrey, then director of the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy, concluded it could not be classified as an anabolic steroid because there was no proof it built muscle.[1] The IOC banned it in 1997, and the FDA banned sales on April 11, 2004.[1]

The Anabolic Steroid Control Act, introduced March 12, 2004, took effect on January 20, 2005, and placed anabolic steroids and prohormones under the Controlled Substances Act. Androstenedione is a Schedule III substance in the US.[1]

Androstenedione is a weak androgen produced in the adrenal glands and gonads. It can be converted to testosterone by 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, or to estrone by aromatase.[1] Reviews of hormones and hair follicles describe androstenedione and DHEAS as prohormones of testosterone and DHT, the androgens that drive terminal hair growth.[6]

A 2000 JAMA study found that a single 300 mg oral dose raised serum testosterone in young men over eight hours, while a 100 mg dose had no significant effect, and estradiol rose at both doses with wide individual variation.[1] A 2006 review by Brown, Vukovich and King found that daily doses of 50 or 100 mg had no effect on strength, muscle size or body fat; the authors raised the possibility that higher doses might act differently while noting variable responses and unknown risks.[1]
A sports-science review of dietary supplements noted that few products used by athletes are supported by a sound research base and that some may be harmful.[7]

A study of 10 healthy women given 100 mg reported voice deepening, increased body hair, menstrual irregularities and abnormal bleeding, blood clots and metabolic disruption, according to a 2021 review summarized on Wikipedia.[1]

An international analysis bought 634 non-hormonal supplements in 13 countries between 2000 and 2001, following earlier reports that some supplements contained undeclared prohormones.[8] Anti-doping authorities cite this contamination risk when warning athletes.

Androstenedione is prohibited by WADA, the Olympics, and major leagues including MLB, the NFL, the NBA and the NCAA.[1] Its association with the McGwire home-run era continues to appear in T Nation discussions of steroids in sport.[9] A 2002 review, "Prohormones and sport," addressed the topic in the steroid biochemistry literature.[10]

Human studies of androstenedione include the 2000 JAMA study of testosterone response in young men and a 2006 review of strength and body composition outcomes, summarized above.[1] A 2004 multi-country analysis tested supplements for undeclared anabolic steroids.[8] No studies of 1-androstenedione were located.

timeline.event: White House drug-policy director Barry McCaffrey begins a review, concluding by 2001 that andro could not be classed as an anabolic steroid.[1]
A JAMA study measures testosterone response to oral androstenedione in young men.[1]
The FDA bans sale on April 11; the Anabolic Steroid Control Act is introduced March 12.[1]
The Anabolic Steroid Control Act takes effect January 20.[1]

lore.intro: Prohormones are remembered in bodybuilding communities as the legal pro-steroid supplements of the 1990s and 2000s, and T Nation members still trade stories about them.[2][4]

claims.claim: Andro raises testosterone and builds muscle
claims.believers: Users and sellers in the supplement era said it acted like a mild steroid, and posters recall classmates who used prohormones.[2][5]
claims.experts: A 2006 review found 50 to 100 mg daily had no effect on strength, muscle size or body fat; a 300 mg dose raised testosterone variably.[1]

claims.claim: Prohormones are a legal alternative to steroids
claims.believers: Supplement marketing positioned them as legal and mild; some T Nation posters describe using designer prohormones before moving on to injectable compounds.[11]
claims.experts: The FDA banned androstenedione in 2004 and the US classed it as a controlled anabolic steroid; reported effects in women included masculinization.[1]

claims.claim: Over-the-counter prohormone products are often underdosed
claims.believers: One T Nation poster describes brand-name prohormones as underdosed and expensive.[12]
claims.experts: A 2000 to 2001 international analysis examined 634 supplements for undeclared anabolic steroids.[8]
